items.stem: Which pillars are usually included in sustainable development?
items.answer: Environmental, social and economic
items.markingKey: Environmental, social and economic. The three pillars (Brundtland, 1987; often shown as overlapping circles).

items.stem: A student claims: "Sustainability means not using natural resources at all." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Sustainability allows use, provided harvests do not exceed natural income and ecosystems can fully recover.
items.markingKey: Sustainability allows use, provided harvests do not exceed natural income and ecosystems can fully recover. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between natural capital and natural income.
items.answer: Natural capital is the stock (e.g. a forest); natural income is the flow it yields each year (e.g. annual timber growth). Living off income keeps capital intact; consuming capital is unsustainable.
items.markingKey: Natural capital is the stock (e.g. a forest); natural income is the flow it yields each year (e.g. annual timber growth). Living off income keeps capital intact; consuming capital is unsustainable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (Costa Rica's payments for ecosystem services (PSA, since 1997)): Landowners are paid to protect forest, funded partly by a fuel tax; forest cover rose from about 21% in the 1980s to over 50% by 2020.

Explain what this information reveals about valuing natural capital.
items.answer: Paying for regulating services (carbon, water, biodiversity, scenery) gives landowners an incentive to conserve natural capital.
items.markingKey: Paying for regulating services (carbon, water, biodiversity, scenery) gives landowners an incentive to conserve natural capital. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to valuing natural capital, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.answer: Landowners are paid to protect forest, funded partly by a fuel tax; forest cover rose from about 21% in the 1980s to over 50% by 2020. Paying for regulating services (carbon, water, biodiversity, scenery) gives landowners an incentive to conserve natural capital.

items.stem: Explain the consequences of consuming natural capital rather than natural income, referring in detail to the collapse of the Grand Banks cod fishery, Newfoundland and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]
items.answer: Catches peaked at about 800,000 t in 1968; the stock collapsed by over 95% and a moratorium in 1992 put about 35,000 people out of work. Catches far above sustainable yield depleted the stock itself, removing the income on which the industry depended; recovery has been very slow. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Catches peaked at about 800,000 t in 1968; the stock collapsed by over 95% and a moratorium in 1992 put about 35,000 people out of work. Catches far above sustainable yield depleted the stock itself, removing the income on which the industry depended; recovery has been very slow. [7]: award [1] per valid, developed point up to [7]; credit accurate terminology, the mechanism or process, specific detail from the named example(s) and explicit links to the question; max [4] if no specific example.

items.answer: Helps: makes values visible (Dasgupta Review, natural capital accounting in UK/China GEP), supports PES; hinders: anthropocentric framing, commodification, valuation uncertainty, ignores intrinsic value. Judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Helps: makes values visible (Dasgupta Review, natural capital accounting in UK/China GEP), supports PES; hinders: anthropocentric framing, commodification, valuation uncertainty, ignores intrinsic value. items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Putting a monetary value on ecosystem services is the best way to protect natural capital."
items.answer: Valuation is a useful tool for decision-making, but should complement legal protection and recognition of intrinsic value.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: makes hidden values visible in decisions (Costanza 1997 ~US$33 trillion/yr); enables payment schemes (Costa Rica PSA). Limitations / counter-points: some values (intrinsic, spiritual) cannot be priced; risks commodifying nature; valuations are uncertain; markets may still trade nature away if a higher price is offered. Conclusion: Valuation is a useful tool for decision-making, but should complement legal protection and recognition of intrinsic value. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: Explain why natural capital is not always valued in economic decisions.
items.answer: Many ecosystem services (climate regulation, pollination) are public goods with no market price, so they are treated as free externalities; GDP counts depletion of natural capital as income.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many ecosystem services (climate regulation, pollination) are public goods with no market price, so they are treated as free externalities; GDP counts depletion of natural capital as income. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline why sustainability requires consideration of social and economic as well as environmental factors.
items.answer: Policies that ignore livelihoods, equity or costs fail politically or push activities elsewhere; long-term environmental health depends on people being able to meet needs and having incentives to conserve.
items.markingKey: Policies that ignore livelihoods, equity or costs fail politically or push activities elsewhere; long-term environmental health depends on people being able to meet needs and having incentives to conserve. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Suggest two indicators that could show whether a forest is managed sustainably.
items.answer: Standing stock / area of forest stable or increasing over time; harvest ≤ annual increment; biodiversity indicators stable; soil quality maintained; certification (FSC).
items.markingKey: Standing stock / area of forest stable or increasing over time; harvest ≤ annual increment; biodiversity indicators stable; soil quality maintained; certification (FSC).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "biocapacity"?
options: An action taken to avoid, reduce or compensate for negative impacts of a development
The view that natural capital cannot be replaced by human-made capital and must be maintained
The outer ring of the doughnut model, based on the nine planetary boundaries, beyond which environmental degradation threatens human wellbeing
The capacity of a given biologically productive area to generate a supply of renewable resources and to absorb its wastes
items.answer: The capacity of a given biologically productive area to generate a supply of renewable resources and to absorb its wastes
items.markingKey: D. "biocapacity" is the capacity of a given biologically productive area to generate a supply of renewable resources and to absorb its wastes.

items.stem: Outline two limitations of the ecological footprint as a sustainability indicator.
items.answer: It omits some impacts (freshwater use, toxic pollution, biodiversity loss); it assumes current technology and yields; converting carbon to forest area is hypothetical; data for some countries are poor.
items.markingKey: It omits some impacts (freshwater use, toxic pollution, biodiversity loss); it assumes current technology and yields; converting carbon to forest area is hypothetical; data for some countries are poor. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Explain the difference between ecological footprint and carbon footprint.
items.answer: The ecological footprint is expressed in global hectares and includes cropland, grazing, forest, fishing, built-up land and carbon; a carbon footprint measures only greenhouse-gas emissions, in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent.
items.markingKey: The ecological footprint is expressed in global hectares and includes cropland, grazing, forest, fishing, built-up land and carbon; a carbon footprint measures only greenhouse-gas emissions, in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A country with a small ecological footprint per person must have a small total footprint." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Total footprint = per-capita footprint × population; China and India have modest per-capita footprints but large totals.
items.markingKey: Total footprint = per-capita footprint × population; China and India have modest per-capita footprints but large totals. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Compare the ecological footprint per person of Qatar (about 14 gha) with India (about 1.2 gha) and suggest reasons for the difference.
items.answer: Qatar's is roughly 12 times larger due to high incomes, energy-intensive air conditioning and desalination, cheap fossil fuels, high car use and imports of food; India has lower incomes and consumption.
items.markingKey: Qatar's is roughly 12 times larger due to high incomes, energy-intensive air conditioning and desalination, cheap fossil fuels, high car use and imports of food; India has lower incomes and consumption.

items.stem: To what extent can individual lifestyle choices reduce a country's ecological footprint? [9]
items.answer: Individual choices: diet, travel, energy, consumption (e.g. plant-based diet can cut food footprint by about half); limits: infrastructure, energy mix, industry and government policy dominate; rebound effects; need for structural change. Judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Individual choices: diet, travel, energy, consumption (e.g. plant-based diet can cut food footprint by about half); limits: infrastructure, energy mix, industry and government policy dominate; rebound effects; need for structural change. items.stem: In recent years humanity has used resources at a rate equivalent to about how many Earths?
items.answer: About 1.7
items.markingKey: C. Global Footprint Network estimates ~1.7 Earths; Earth Overshoot Day fell on 1 August in 2024.

items.stem: Explain the difference between biocapacity and ecological footprint.
items.answer: Ecological footprint measures demand: the productive area needed to supply a population's consumption and absorb its waste; biocapacity measures supply: the productive area available. Footprint > biocapacity is an ecological deficit.
items.markingKey: Ecological footprint measures demand: the productive area needed to supply a population's consumption and absorb its waste; biocapacity measures supply: the productive area available. Footprint > biocapacity is an ecological deficit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Singapore, explain how it illustrates dependence on imported biocapacity.
items.answer: A city-state with a footprint of about 5-6 gha per person but biocapacity close to 0.1 gha per person. Almost all food, water and energy are imported, so the city relies on other countries' land and on trade.

items.answer: It is a useful headline indicator but must be combined with others (water footprint, planetary boundaries, HDI) for a full picture.

items.stem: According to the 2023 update (Richardson et al.), how many of the nine planetary boundaries had been transgressed?
items.answer: Six
items.markingKey: B. Climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows and novel entities.

items.stem: Explain one limitation of the planetary boundaries model.
items.answer: Boundaries are global but impacts are local; thresholds are uncertain; some processes (novel entities) are hard to quantify; it does not address who is responsible or social equity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Boundaries are global but impacts are local; thresholds are uncertain; some processes (novel entities) are hard to quantify; it does not address who is responsible or social equity. items.stem: State two differences between the planetary boundaries model and the doughnut economics model.
items.answer: Planetary boundaries define environmental limits only; the doughnut adds a social foundation, so it identifies a space that is both ecologically safe and socially just.
items.markingKey: Planetary boundaries define environmental limits only; the doughnut adds a social foundation, so it identifies a space that is both ecologically safe and socially just. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Suggest two policies a city could adopt to move into the "safe and just space" of the doughnut.
items.answer: e.g. circular-economy procurement and repair hubs (reduce material use); affordable, energy-efficient social housing (meets social foundation while cutting emissions); public transport and cycling investment.
items.markingKey: e.g. circular-economy procurement and repair hubs (reduce material use); affordable, energy-efficient social housing (meets social foundation while cutting emissions); public transport and cycling investment.

items.stem:
Study the extract from the resource booklet.

Data (O'Neill et al., 2018) for 150 countries: no country met all 11 social thresholds without transgressing at least some biophysical boundaries; Vietnam met 6 social thresholds while transgressing only 1 boundary; the USA met 11 social thresholds but transgressed 7 boundaries.

Suggest one way a country like Vietnam could improve its social outcomes without crossing more boundaries.
items.answer: Invest in renewable energy, public health and education (low resource intensity), efficient public transport and sustainable agriculture rather than copying high-consumption development.
items.markingKey: Invest in renewable energy, public health and education (low resource intensity), efficient public transport and sustainable agriculture rather than copying high-consumption development. items.stem: Noah writes: "If a planetary boundary is crossed, catastrophic collapse happens immediately." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Crossing a boundary moves into a zone of increasing risk; the boundary is set before suspected tipping points, so effects may be gradual and uncertain.

items.stem: "The SDGs only apply to low-income countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The SDGs are universal and apply to all UN member states, including high-income countries (e.g. SDG 12 responsible consumption).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a strategic environmental assessment and an EIA.
items.answer: An EIA assesses one project (e.g. a dam); a strategic environmental assessment assesses a whole policy, plan or programme (e.g. a national energy plan), so it can address cumulative impacts earlier.
items.markingKey: An EIA assesses one project (e.g. a dam); a strategic environmental assessment assesses a whole policy, plan or programme (e.g. a national energy plan), so it can address cumulative impacts earlier. items.stem: Identify two SDGs most relevant to a project to restore mangroves and explain one link for each.
items.answer: SDG 14 (nursery habitat for fish), SDG 13 (blue-carbon storage and storm protection), SDG 1/8 (livelihoods from fisheries and ecotourism).

items.answer: Progress on one goal affects others: e.g. clean energy (SDG 7) supports climate action (SDG 13) and health (SDG 3), but agricultural expansion for zero hunger (SDG 2) may conflict with life on land (SDG 15).

items.stem: Which statement best describes the sustainable use of a forest?
options: Harvesting the oldest trees as fast as possible
Harvesting no more than its annual growth so the stock is maintained
Banning all use of the forest
Clear-felling and replanting with a different species
items.answer: Harvesting no more than its annual growth so the stock is maintained

items.stem: The natural capital of a seaweed farm in Zanzibar grows from 719 to 815 tonnes of seaweed per farm in 4 year(s) without harvesting. A manager proposes harvesting 28.8 tonnes of seaweed per farm each year. (a) Calculate the sustainable yield. (b) Assuming constant growth, calculate the stock after 10 years of the proposed harvest and state whether it is sustainable. (c) Explain why sustainable yield is hard to set in practice.
items.answer: (a) 24.0 tonnes of seaweed per farm per year (b) 719 + (24.0 − 28.8) × 10 = 671; unsustainable (natural capital declining) (c) growth rates vary with climate, disease and stock size (density dependence); data are uncertain; economic pressure favours over-setting quotas; time lags in monitoring.

items.stem: With reference to Singapore, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in dependence on imported biocapacity. [7]
items.answer: A city-state with a footprint of about 5-6 gha per person but biocapacity close to 0.1 gha per person. Almost all food, water and energy are imported, so the city relies on other countries' land and on trade. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: With reference to Amsterdam's City Doughnut (2020), explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in applying the doughnut model to policy. [7]
items.answer: The city used the doughnut model to plan its circular strategy, aiming to halve use of new raw materials by 2030 and be fully circular by 2050. It translates global social and ecological limits into local targets for housing, materials and emissions. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: With reference to the Three Gorges Dam EIA, China, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in the difficulty of predicting impacts. [7]
items.answer: A 1991 environmental assessment predicted sedimentation and biodiversity impacts; after completion, landslides around the reservoir, downstream erosion and declining Yangtze fisheries were reported. Some impacts were underestimated or cumulative, showing the need for monitoring after construction. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Putting a monetary value on ecosystem services is the best way to protect natural capital."
items.answer: Valuation is a useful tool for decision-making, but should complement legal protection and recognition of intrinsic value.
items.markingKey: For: makes hidden values visible in decisions (Costanza 1997 ~US$33 trillion/yr). Against: some values (intrinsic, spiritual) cannot be priced. items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that the ecological footprint is the best measure of a country's environmental sustainability.
items.answer: It is a useful headline indicator but must be combined with others (water footprint, planetary boundaries, HDI) for a full picture.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: single, easily communicated figure; compares demand with supply; tracks change over time. items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "The planetary boundaries framework is a useful guide for global environmental policy."
items.answer: It is a powerful communication and agenda-setting tool, but must be downscaled and combined with equity considerations to guide policy.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "strong sustainability"?
options: A hectare with world-average biological productivity, used as the unit of ecological footprints and biocapacity
A framework (Rockström et al., 2009) of nine Earth-system processes with thresholds that define a safe operating space for humanity
The stock of natural resources and ecosystems, such as forests, soils, fish stocks and aquifers, that yields goods and services
The view that natural capital cannot be replaced by human-made capital and must be maintained
items.answer: The view that natural capital cannot be replaced by human-made capital and must be maintained
items.markingKey: D. "strong sustainability" is the view that natural capital cannot be replaced by human-made capital and must be maintained.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The area of land and water required to sustainably provide all the resources at the rate at which they are being consumed by a given population and to absorb its wastes, measured in global hectares"?
items.answer: ecological footprint (EF)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of ecological footprint (EF).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "safe operating space"?
options: The range within the planetary boundaries in which humanity can develop without destabilising Earth's systems
The stock of natural resources and ecosystems, such as forests, soils, fish stocks and aquifers, that yields goods and services
A report prepared before a development project that assesses its likely environmental, social and economic impacts, considers alternatives and proposes mitigation
The area of land and water required to sustainably provide all the resources at the rate at which they are being consumed by a given population and to absorb its wastes, measured in global hectares
items.answer: The range within the planetary boundaries in which humanity can develop without destabilising Earth's systems
items.markingKey: A. "safe operating space" is the range within the planetary boundaries in which humanity can develop without destabilising Earth's systems.

items.stem: Briefly explain why baseline studies are essential in an EIA.
items.answer: They record the state of habitats, species, water, air and communities before development so impacts can be predicted, monitored and compared; without a baseline, change cannot be measured or attributed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They record the state of habitats, species, water, air and communities before development so impacts can be predicted, monitored and compared; without a baseline, change cannot be measured or attributed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the concept of natural income can be used to manage a fishery sustainably.
items.answer: The fish stock is natural capital; recruitment and growth each year are natural income; setting catches at or below the sustainable yield (e.g. MSY or lower) maintains the stock.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The fish stock is natural capital; recruitment and growth each year are natural income; setting catches at or below the sustainable yield (e.g. MSY or lower) maintains the stock. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how a country can have a footprint larger than its biocapacity.
items.answer: It imports resources produced on other countries' land, emits CO₂ absorbed by the global commons, and may deplete its own natural capital (overfishing, groundwater mining).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It imports resources produced on other countries' land, emits CO₂ absorbed by the global commons, and may deplete its own natural capital (overfishing, groundwater mining). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "If a planetary boundary is crossed, catastrophic collapse happens immediately." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Crossing a boundary moves into a zone of increasing risk; the boundary is set before suspected tipping points, so effects may be gradual and uncertain.
items.markingKey: Crossing a boundary moves into a zone of increasing risk; the boundary is set before suspected tipping points, so effects may be gradual and uncertain. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Millennium Development Goals and the Sustainable Development Goals.
items.answer: The 8 MDGs (2000-2015) focused mainly on poverty and health in low-income countries; the 17 SDGs (2015-2030) are universal, apply to all countries and integrate environmental, social and economic sustainability.
items.markingKey: The 8 MDGs (2000-2015) focused mainly on poverty and health in low-income countries; the 17 SDGs (2015-2030) are universal, apply to all countries and integrate environmental, social and economic sustainability. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between strong sustainability and weak sustainability.
items.answer: Strong sustainability holds that critical natural capital cannot be substituted and must be conserved; weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by human-made capital as long as total capital is maintained.
items.markingKey: Strong sustainability holds that critical natural capital cannot be substituted and must be conserved; weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by human-made capital as long as total capital is maintained. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Ecological footprint and biocapacity (gha per person, Global Footprint Network, approximate): USA EF 8.0, BC 3.4; China EF 3.6, BC 0.9; India EF 1.2, BC 0.4; Brazil EF 2.6, BC 8.1; Japan EF 4.4, BC 0.6.

items.answer: Brazil (8.1 > 2.6); USA deficit = 8.0 − 3.4 = 4.6 gha per person.

Case study extract - the Gulf of Mexico dead zone: Nitrogen and phosphorus from Mississippi basin farmland create a hypoxic zone averaging about 14,000 km² each summer.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates transgression of the biogeochemical flows boundary.
items.answer: Excess fertiliser nutrients overload the ocean, causing eutrophication and oxygen loss far from where the fertiliser was applied.

items.answer: Population growth (more people sharing the stock); deforestation, soil degradation, overfishing and biodiversity loss.
